title: 3-Read Friday #70: Atomisation, Girls and Learning, and Scripted Lessons
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #70 of 3-Read Friday continues the atomisation debate Barton stirred up with Kris Boulton the previous week, this time linking to Colin Foster's counter-argument for connected, non-atomised approaches to teaching multi-step maths processes -- a piece Barton says he wants to bring both authors on his podcast to debate directly. Rebecca Birch follows with a review of five popular claims about how girls learn differently, presented at the International Coalition of Girls Schools conference, testing folk beliefs like learning styles and collaborative preference against the evidence. Greg Ashman closes the issue defending scripted, centrally-planned lessons against a recent critique, describing how his team's iterative, data-driven refinement process addresses the usual objections to prescribed curricula. Barton frames the issue around productive disagreement -- Foster versus Boulton on atomisation, evidence versus folk wisdom on girls' learning, and Ashman's rebuttal to scripted-lesson skeptics -- as a demonstration that good ideas in education should be argued out, not simply asserted.
points: Foster's direct rebuttal to Boulton's atomisation framework (both linked in consecutive 3-Read Friday issues) gives readers a genuine head-to-head disagreement between two credentialed voices on the same specific pedagogical question.

Birch's conference-presentation review tests five specific claims about girls' learning against research evidence, debunking VARK-style learning-styles claims while finding partial truth in fragility-related concerns.

Ashman's defense of scripted lessons centers on iteration: his team continuously revises centrally-planned lessons based on classroom data, directly countering the common objection that scripted curricula are static and unresponsive.

Barton's explicit framing -- wanting to bring Foster and Boulton onto his podcast to debate -- signals he's treating 3-Read Friday's role as surfacing live disagreements rather than only settled conclusions.
quotes: I always like to be challenged, and following my podcast with atomisation advocate Kris Boulton, Colin Foster sent me this piece that argues against breaking all maths down into atoms.
I think I need to get Colin and Kris on the podcast to hash this out!

Rebecca analyses the evidence supporting several claims about the difference between how girls and boys learn (Girls Learn Better Collaboratively, Girls Are Better Off Educated With Boys) and reaches some fascinating conclusions.
Greg responds to a recent critique of centrally planned lessons.
The way Greg and his team systematically iterate and improve their lessons based on data is something all departments could aspire towards.
